sections.s6_takeaway:
Delta Lake gives me a set of maintenance and read-acceleration operations that I treat as standard housekeeping for any busy table. OPTIMIZE compacts many small files into fewer large ones, which fixes the small-file problem that streaming and frequent appends create, since each tiny file carries real open-and-read overhead. ZORDER BY physically clusters rows that share values in the chosen columns, and VACUUM reclaims data files that the transaction log no longer references once they are older than the retention window. Optimized writes and auto-compaction reduce small files right at write time so I need less manual OPTIMIZE later.

The engine that makes all of this pay off is data skipping. Whenever Delta writes a data file, it records per-file minimum and maximum statistics for each column in the transaction log. When a query filters on a column, Delta checks each file's min and max for that column, and if the filter value falls outside a file's range, it skips that file entirely without reading a single byte. ZORDER makes those ranges tight and non-overlapping on the columns people actually filter by, so the fraction of files skipped goes way up. I ZORDER on high-cardinality filter columns like account id, and I use partitioning for low-cardinality columns like region.

At the National Bank of India this was the difference between a dashboard that timed out and one that returned instantly. Our card stream produced thousands of tiny files a day, so a nightly OPTIMIZE with ZORDER on account id compacted them and clustered each account's rows together. After that, a query for a single account's history read only the one file whose min and max actually covered that account, and the rest were skipped on their statistics alone. We then ran VACUUM with the default seven-day retention to reclaim the dead files safely without breaking in-flight readers or recent time travel. The line I give in interviews is that OPTIMIZE compacts, ZORDER clusters, min and max statistics drive skipping, and VACUUM reclaims — and skipping is the part that actually makes the queries fast.

answers.question: What is Delta Lake time travel (`VERSION AS OF n`, `TIMESTAMP AS OF ts`) — reading historical versions of a table — and what are its use cases (debugging, audit, rollback, reproducible ML)?
answers.shortTitle: Delta Lake time travel

s1_definition.profdef: Delta Lake time travel is the ability to read a table as it existed at a past version or point in time, using `VERSION AS OF n` or `TIMESTAMP AS OF ts` in SQL, or the `versionAsOf` and `timestampAsOf` read options in the DataFrame API. It works because every write commits a new, immutable version in the transaction log and the underlying data files for old versions remain until VACUUM removes them. Primary use cases are debugging, auditing, rollback of bad writes, and reproducible machine learning.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank's ledger is append-only and numbered. If someone asks "what was Rajesh's balance table at 9 AM, before the correction batch ran?", you do not need a backup — you just flip the ledger back to that page. Delta's log is exactly that numbered ledger; time travel is flipping back to any page by version number or timestamp.
s1_definition.oneliner: Time travel reads any past version of a Delta table by version number or timestamp, because every commit is kept as an immutable snapshot.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Delta Lake time travel is the ability to read a table as it existed at a past version or point in time, using `VERSION AS OF n` or `TIMESTAMP AS OF ts` in SQL, or the `versionAsOf` and `timestampAsOf` read options in the DataFrame API. It works because every write commits a new, immutable version in the transaction log and the underlying data files for old versions remain until VACUUM removes them. Primary use cases are debugging, auditing, rollback of bad writes, and reproducible machine learning.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank's ledger is append-only and numbered. If someone asks "what was Rajesh's balance table at 9 AM, before the correction batch ran?", you do not need a backup — you just flip the ledger back to that page. Delta's log is exactly that numbered ledger; time travel is flipping back to any page by version number or timestamp.

**One line to remember:** Time travel reads any past version of a Delta table by version number or timestamp, because every commit is kept as an immutable snapshot.

sections.s2_technical:
Every Delta write produces a new version N with its own commit file in `_delta_log`. The commit records which files were added and removed, but the removed files stay on disk until VACUUM deletes them after the retention window. Time travel reconstructs the file set for a chosen version by replaying the log only up to that point.

In SQL you write `SELECT * FROM delta.\`/path\` VERSION AS OF 3` or `SELECT * FROM delta.\`/path\` TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-10-30 09:00:00'`. In the DataFrame API you use `spark.read.format("delta").option("versionAsOf", 3).load(path)` or `.option("timestampAsOf", "2026-10-30 09:00:00")`. The timestamp variant maps to the latest commit at or before that time.

For debugging, you compare a known-good version with a suspect one to see exactly what a job changed. For audit, you reproduce the precise state a report was based on, which regulators often demand. For rollback, you restore a table to a prior good version using `RESTORE TABLE delta.\`/path\` TO VERSION AS OF n`, which creates a new commit whose data equals the old version rather than deleting history. For reproducible machine learning, you pin a training read to a fixed version so a model is always trained on identical data, making experiments repeatable.

A senior nuance: time travel only works within the retention window, because VACUUM eventually removes old files; if you must keep a version forever, clone it or archive it. Also, timestamp-based reads can be surprising around clock boundaries, so for strict reproducibility prefer version numbers.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A correction batch accidentally overwrote part of the National Bank's balances table with wrong values. The operations team needs to see the table exactly as it was before the batch to understand the damage. This is exactly what time travel's `VERSION AS OF` gives us.

Problem 2 — An auditor asks the bank to reproduce the end-of-day balance report from a specific timestamp. This is exactly the `TIMESTAMP AS OF` use case.

Problem 3 — The bad write must be undone without losing audit history. This is exactly what `RESTORE TO VERSION AS OF` does — it rolls forward to a state equal to the old version.

What the code will do: a PySpark demo (`TimeTravelDemo`) that creates a balances table, makes a good write and then a bad overwrite, reads the earlier version, reads by timestamp, and restores the table to the good version — for Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001).

```python
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s")

            .config("spark.sql.extensions", "io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension")

                    "org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog")
            .getOrCreate())

def main() -> None:
    spark = spark_session()

    # Version 0: correct balances
    good = spark.createDataFrame(
        [("SAV2001", "Rajesh Kumar", Decimal("1000000.00")),
         ("CUR3001", "Priya Sharma", Decimal("250000.00"))],
        ["account_id", "holder_name", "balance"])
    good.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").save(PATH)
    log.info("Version 0 written (correct balances)")

    # Version 1: a BAD overwrite zeros out balances by mistake
    bad = spark.createDataFrame(
        [("SAV2001", "Rajesh Kumar", Decimal("0.00")),
         ("CUR3001", "Priya Sharma", Decimal("0.00"))],
        ["account_id", "holder_name", "balance"])
    bad.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").save(PATH)
    log.warning("Version 1 written (BAD overwrite - balances zeroed)")

    reader = VersionReader(spark, PATH)
    log.info("Current (bad) state:")
    reader.current().show()
    log.info("Time travel VERSION AS OF 0 (pre-bug):")
    reader.at_version(0).show()

    reader.restore_to_version(0)                 # roll forward to good state
    log.info("After RESTORE TO VERSION 0:")
```

```python
# File: src/history/version_reader.py
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, DataFrame

class VersionReader:
    """Reads historical versions and restores a Delta table."""
    def __init__(self, spark: SparkSession, path: str):
        self.spark = spark
        self.path = path

    def current(self) -> DataFrame:
        return self.spark.read.format("delta").load(self.path)

    def at_version(self, version: int) -> DataFrame:
        return (self.spark.read.format("delta")
                .option("versionAsOf", version).load(self.path))

    def at_timestamp(self, ts: str) -> DataFrame:
        return (self.spark.read.format("delta")
                .option("timestampAsOf", ts).load(self.path))

    def restore_to_version(self, version: int) -> None:
        # RESTORE creates a NEW commit equal to the old version (history preserved)
        self.spark.sql(
            f"RESTORE TABLE delta.`{self.path}` TO VERSION AS OF {version}")
```

Input data: correct balances at version 0, then a bad overwrite at version 1.

Step 1: The good write creates version 0 with Rajesh at 1,000,000 and Priya at 250,000. The log records the add of the data files.

Step 3: `reader.current()` reads the latest version and shows the zeros — the damage.

Step 4: `reader.at_version(0)` replays the log only to version 0, so Delta uses the still-present original files and shows the correct balances.

Step 5: `restore_to_version(0)` writes a new commit (version 2) whose data equals version 0. History is preserved: versions 0, 1, and 2 all remain readable.

Step 6: `reader.current()` now shows the restored correct balances.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Delta Lake time travel is the ability to read a table exactly as it existed at a past version or point in time. In SQL I use VERSION AS OF a number or TIMESTAMP AS OF a timestamp, and in the DataFrame API I use the versionAsOf and timestampAsOf read options. It works because every write commits a new, immutable version in the transaction log, and the data files for older versions stay on disk until VACUUM removes them after the retention window. To read an old version, Delta simply replays the log up to that point and uses the file set that was valid then.

The use cases I lean on are debugging, auditing, rollback, and reproducible machine learning. For debugging I compare a known-good version against a suspect one to see precisely what a job changed. For auditing I reproduce the exact state a report was computed from, which regulators frequently demand. For rollback I use RESTORE TABLE TO VERSION AS OF, which writes a new commit whose data equals the old version, so I recover without destroying history. And for machine learning I pin a training read to a fixed version so a model always trains on identical data and experiments stay reproducible.

At the National Bank of India this saved us during an incident where a correction batch overwrote part of the balances table with wrong values. Instead of restoring from a nightly backup and losing hours of other writes, I read the table with VERSION AS OF the pre-batch version to see the correct balances, confirmed the damage, and then ran RESTORE to roll the table forward to that good state while keeping every version in the audit trail. When an auditor later asked for an end-of-day report from a specific moment, I answered with a TIMESTAMP AS OF read. The caution I always add is that time travel only works inside the retention window, so if a version must live forever I clone or archive it, and for strict reproducibility I prefer version numbers over timestamps.

answers.question: What is Delta Lake's `MERGE INTO` (upsert) — atomically match rows and INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE in one statement — and how does it compare to a manual read-check-write pattern (MERGE is atomic and handles concurrency)?
answers.shortTitle: Delta Lake MERGE INTO (upsert)

s1_definition.profdef: `MERGE INTO` is Delta Lake's atomic upsert operation. It joins a target table with a source dataset on a matching condition and, in a single transaction, applies `WHEN MATCHED` actions (UPDATE or DELETE) and `WHEN NOT MATCHED` actions (INSERT). Because it commits as one Delta transaction, it is atomic and isolated, unlike a hand-written read-check-then-write sequence that can race with concurrent writers and leave the table inconsistent.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank gets a nightly file of balance changes. For each account, if it already exists, update the balance; if it is new, insert it; if it is closed, delete it. Doing this by hand means reading each account, checking, then writing — and if two clerks do this at once, they can overwrite each other. `MERGE INTO` is one clerk who does the whole match-and-apply in a single locked step, so the result is always correct.
s1_definition.oneliner: MERGE INTO is a single atomic upsert that matches source to target and applies UPDATE, DELETE, and INSERT together, safely under concurrency.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `MERGE INTO` is Delta Lake's atomic upsert operation. It joins a target table with a source dataset on a matching condition and, in a single transaction, applies `WHEN MATCHED` actions (UPDATE or DELETE) and `WHEN NOT MATCHED` actions (INSERT). Because it commits as one Delta transaction, it is atomic and isolated, unlike a hand-written read-check-then-write sequence that can race with concurrent writers and leave the table inconsistent.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank gets a nightly file of balance changes. For each account, if it already exists, update the balance; if it is new, insert it; if it is closed, delete it. Doing this by hand means reading each account, checking, then writing — and if two clerks do this at once, they can overwrite each other. `MERGE INTO` is one clerk who does the whole match-and-apply in a single locked step, so the result is always correct.

**One line to remember:** MERGE INTO is a single atomic upsert that matches source to target and applies UPDATE, DELETE, and INSERT together, safely under concurrency.

sections.s2_technical:
A MERGE has three parts: the target Delta table, the source DataFrame or table, and an ON condition that defines a match (usually a business key). Then you specify branches. `WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET ...` updates existing rows, `WHEN MATCHED THEN DELETE` removes them, and `WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT ...` adds new rows. You can add conditions to branches, for example `WHEN MATCHED AND source.status = 'CLOSED' THEN DELETE`.

In the DataFrame API it reads naturally: `DeltaTable.forPath(spark, path).alias("t").merge(source.alias("s"), "t.account_id = s.account_id").whenMatchedUpdate(set={"balance": "s.balance"}).whenNotMatchedInsertAll().execute()`.

The contrast with a manual pattern is the key interview point. A manual upsert reads the target, computes which rows to update or insert in the driver or another job, and writes them back. Between the read and the write, another writer can change the table, so your write is based on stale state and you lose updates or create duplicates. MERGE avoids this because Delta performs the join and the writes inside one optimistic transaction, detecting conflicting commits and failing or retrying rather than silently corrupting data. It is also far more efficient, rewriting only the files that contain matched rows rather than the whole table.

A senior nuance: MERGE can be expensive if the match condition touches many files, so you narrow it with partition or ZORDER predicates and avoid multiple matches per target row, which Delta rejects to keep results deterministic. You also use `whenNotMatchedBySourceDelete` to remove target rows absent from the source when doing full-sync upserts.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank receives a nightly change file: some accounts have new balances, some are brand new, and some are closed. Applying this with a read-check-write loop risks losing concurrent updates. This is exactly what MERGE's atomic upsert solves.

Problem 2 — New accounts must be inserted, existing ones updated, and closed ones deleted, all in one pass. This maps directly to the three MERGE branches.

Problem 3 — The operation must be safe even if another job writes to the same table at the same time. This is the concurrency and atomicity guarantee MERGE provides over a manual pattern.

What the code will do: a PySpark demo (`MergeUpsertDemo`) that starts with a balances table for Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001), then applies a change file that updates Rajesh, inserts a new account, and closes Priya — all in one MERGE.

```sql
    account_id STRING, balance DECIMAL(15,2), status STRING

USING changes s
ON t.account_id = s.account_id
WHEN MATCHED AND s.status = 'CLOSED' THEN DELETE
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET t.balance = s.balance, t.status = s.status
```

```python
# File: src/merge_upsert_demo.py
# Atomic upsert of a nightly change file for the National Bank of India.
import logging
from decimal import Decimal
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from upsert.balance_merger import BalanceMerger

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("MergeUpsertDemo")
PATH = "/data/warehouse/balances_merge"

def spark_session() -> SparkSession:
    return (SparkSession.builder.appName("MergeUpsertDemo")
            .config("spark.sql.extensions", "io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension")
            .config("spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog",
                    "org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog")
            .getOrCreate())

def main() -> None:
    spark = spark_session()
    # Initial target: Rajesh and Priya both ACTIVE
    target = spark.createDataFrame(
        [("SAV2001", Decimal("1000000.00"), "ACTIVE"),
         ("CUR3001", Decimal("250000.00"),  "ACTIVE")],
        ["account_id", "balance", "status"])
    target.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").save(PATH)
    log.info("Initial balances written")

    # Nightly change file: UPDATE Rajesh, INSERT new SAV2002, CLOSE (delete) Priya
    changes = spark.createDataFrame(
        [("SAV2001", Decimal("1050000.00"), "ACTIVE"),   # update
         ("SAV2002", Decimal("75000.00"),   "ACTIVE"),   # insert
         ("CUR3001", Decimal("0.00"),       "CLOSED")],  # delete
        ["account_id", "balance", "status"])

    BalanceMerger(spark, PATH).apply(changes)            # one atomic MERGE
    log.info("After MERGE (upsert):")
    spark.read.format("delta").load(PATH).orderBy("account_id").show()
    spark.stop()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```python
# File: src/upsert/balance_merger.py
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, DataFrame
from delta.tables import DeltaTable

class BalanceMerger:
    """Encapsulates an atomic upsert of balance changes into a Delta table."""
    def __init__(self, spark: SparkSession, path: str):
        self.spark = spark
        self.path = path

    def apply(self, changes: DataFrame) -> None:
        target = DeltaTable.forPath(self.spark, self.path)
        (target.alias("t")
            .merge(changes.alias("s"), "t.account_id = s.account_id")
            # closed accounts are deleted
            .whenMatchedDelete(condition="s.status = 'CLOSED'")
            # existing accounts are updated
            .whenMatchedUpdate(set={"balance": "s.balance", "status": "s.status"})
            # new accounts are inserted
            .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
            .execute())
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
MERGE INTO is Delta Lake's atomic upsert. I give it a target table, a source dataset, and an ON condition that defines what counts as a match, usually a business key. Then I specify branches: WHEN MATCHED can UPDATE or DELETE, and WHEN NOT MATCHED can INSERT, and I can guard each branch with a condition such as deleting only rows whose source status is CLOSED. The whole thing commits as one Delta transaction, so it is atomic and isolated, and it rewrites only the files that actually contain matched rows rather than the whole table.

The reason this matters is the contrast with a hand-written read-check-write pattern. In the manual approach I read the target, figure out which rows to update or insert, and write them back, but between my read and my write another job can change the table, so my write is based on stale state and I either lose updates or create duplicates. MERGE avoids that entirely because Delta performs the join and the writes inside a single optimistic transaction and detects conflicting commits, so it either succeeds cleanly or retries instead of silently corrupting data.

At the National Bank of India we used MERGE for the nightly balance change file. Each night some accounts had new balances, some were brand new, and some were closed, and I applied all three cases in one statement: a matched-and-closed branch that deleted, a matched branch that updated the balance, and a not-matched branch that inserted new accounts. Because it was a single atomic commit, a report running at the same time always saw a consistent snapshot, never a half-applied file. The caution I mention is to keep the match condition narrow using partition or ZORDER predicates so MERGE touches few files, and to make sure the source never matches a target row more than once, since Delta rejects that to keep the result deterministic.

answers.question: Why are plain Python UDFs slow in PySpark — each row is serialized from JVM to Python and back (Py4J/IPC overhead), and Catalyst cannot optimize through the opaque UDF — and what is the performance hierarchy (built-in functions > Pandas UDFs > plain Python UDFs)?
answers.shortTitle: Why plain Python UDFs are slow in PySpark

s1_definition.profdef: A plain Python UDF in PySpark is a user-defined function that Spark invokes once per row. It is slow for two reasons. First, Spark's engine runs on the JVM, so for every row each value must be serialized from JVM memory, sent over an inter-process boundary to a Python worker, deserialized, processed, and serialized back — enormous per-row overhead. Second, the UDF is an opaque black box to the Catalyst optimizer, which cannot see inside it to push down predicates, prune columns, or apply code generation. The performance hierarchy is built-in Spark SQL functions fastest, then vectorized Pandas UDFs, then plain Python UDFs slowest.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank's main ledger is kept by a fast JVM clerk, but you insist every single transaction be mailed to a Python specialist in another building, who opens the envelope, does one calculation, reseals it, and mails it back — one letter per transaction. The postage (serialization) and the round trips dwarf the actual work. A built-in function is the JVM clerk doing it himself. A Pandas UDF mails a whole box of transactions at once instead of one letter each.
s1_definition.oneliner: Plain Python UDFs are slow because every row crosses the JVM-to-Python boundary and the optimizer cannot see inside them — prefer built-ins, then Pandas UDFs.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A plain Python UDF in PySpark is a user-defined function that Spark invokes once per row. It is slow for two reasons. First, Spark's engine runs on the JVM, so for every row each value must be serialized from JVM memory, sent over an inter-process boundary to a Python worker, deserialized, processed, and serialized back — enormous per-row overhead. Second, the UDF is an opaque black box to the Catalyst optimizer, which cannot see inside it to push down predicates, prune columns, or apply code generation. The performance hierarchy is built-in Spark SQL functions fastest, then vectorized Pandas UDFs, then plain Python UDFs slowest.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank's main ledger is kept by a fast JVM clerk, but you insist every single transaction be mailed to a Python specialist in another building, who opens the envelope, does one calculation, reseals it, and mails it back — one letter per transaction. The postage (serialization) and the round trips dwarf the actual work. A built-in function is the JVM clerk doing it himself. A Pandas UDF mails a whole box of transactions at once instead of one letter each.

**One line to remember:** Plain Python UDFs are slow because every row crosses the JVM-to-Python boundary and the optimizer cannot see inside them — prefer built-ins, then Pandas UDFs.

sections.s2_technical:
Spark's core executes on the JVM, and DataFrame columns live in efficient JVM/Tungsten binary format. A plain Python UDF cannot run on the JVM, so Spark launches Python worker processes alongside each executor. For every row, the value is serialized (pickled), handed across the process boundary via sockets using the Py4J/IPC mechanism, deserialized in Python, passed to your function, then serialized back. This per-row serialization and context switching is the dominant cost, often making a UDF tens of times slower than an equivalent built-in.

The second cost is optimizer opacity. Catalyst, Spark's query optimizer, understands built-in functions and can reorder, combine, push filters down to the data source, prune unneeded columns, and generate fused JVM bytecode (whole-stage code generation). A Python UDF is a sealed box: Catalyst must materialize its inputs, call it, and cannot optimize across it. For example a filter that could have been pushed to the Parquet reader now runs after the UDF, scanning far more data.

The performance hierarchy follows from this. Built-in functions such as `F.upper`, `F.when`, and `F.col * F.lit(...)` run entirely on the JVM with full optimization and no boundary crossing, so they are fastest. For example replacing a UDF with `df.withColumn("fee", F.col("amount") * F.lit(0.001))` keeps everything on the JVM. Pandas UDFs (vectorized) transfer data in batches using Apache Arrow and operate on whole columns as pandas Series, amortizing the boundary cost over many rows, so they are typically 10 to 100 times faster than plain UDFs. Plain Python UDFs are the last resort for genuinely row-wise Python logic with no built-in or vectorized equivalent.

A senior nuance: a plain UDF is also non-deterministic to the optimizer by default and blocks predicate pushdown, so even beyond raw speed it changes the query plan for the worse. Always try to express logic with built-ins first, reach for a Pandas UDF when you need custom Python, and use a plain UDF only when neither fits.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank computes a small processing fee on millions of transactions. A developer wrote a plain Python UDF to multiply amount by a rate. On the full dataset it was painfully slow because every one of millions of rows crossed the JVM-to-Python boundary. This is exactly the per-row serialization problem.

Problem 2 — The same logic expressed as a built-in column expression runs entirely on the JVM with optimization. This demonstrates the top of the performance hierarchy.

Problem 3 — Some logic genuinely needs Python (a custom rounding rule from a library). A Pandas UDF processes it in Arrow batches, far faster than row-by-row. This demonstrates the middle tier.

What the code will do: a PySpark demo (`UdfPerfDemo`) that computes a fee on transactions three ways — a plain Python UDF, a built-in expression, and a Pandas UDF — and times each, for Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001) scaled up.

```python
# File: src/udf_perf_demo.py
# Times plain UDF vs built-in vs Pandas UDF for fee calculation at the bank.
import logging, time
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
from fees.fee_calculators import plain_udf_fee, builtin_fee, pandas_udf_fee

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("UdfPerfDemo")

def spark_session() -> SparkSession:
    return (SparkSession.builder.appName("UdfPerfDemo")
            .config("spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled", "true")
            .getOrCreate())

def timed(label, build_df):
    start = time.time()
    count = build_df().count()       # action forces execution
    log.info("%s computed %d rows in %.3fs", label, count, time.time() - start)

def main() -> None:
    spark = spark_session()
    # 2 million synthetic transactions for Rajesh/Priya and others
    base = spark.range(0, 2_000_000).select(
        F.concat(F.lit("TXN-"), F.col("id")).alias("txn_id"),
        F.when(F.col("id") % 2 == 0, F.lit("SAV2001")).otherwise(F.lit("CUR3001"))
            .alias("account_id"),
        (F.col("id") % 100000 + 1000).cast("double").alias("amount"))
    base.cache(); base.count()       # materialize once for fair timing

    timed("PLAIN  Python UDF", lambda: base.withColumn("fee", plain_udf_fee("amount")))
    timed("BUILTIN expression", lambda: base.withColumn("fee", builtin_fee(F.col("amount"))))
    timed("PANDAS UDF        ", lambda: base.withColumn("fee", pandas_udf_fee("amount")))
    spark.stop()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```python
# File: src/fees/fee_calculators.py
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.types import DoubleType
from pyspark.sql.functions import udf, pandas_udf
import pandas as pd

RATE = 0.001

# SLOWEST: plain Python UDF - one row at a time across JVM<->Python boundary
@udf(returnType=DoubleType())
def plain_udf_fee(amount: float) -> float:
    return float(amount) * RATE

# FASTEST: pure built-in column expression - stays on the JVM, fully optimized
def builtin_fee(amount_col):
    return amount_col * F.lit(RATE)

# MIDDLE: vectorized Pandas UDF - Arrow batches, operates on a whole Series
@pandas_udf(DoubleType())
def pandas_udf_fee(amount: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    return amount * RATE
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: 2,000,000 synthetic transactions with an `amount` column.

Step 1: The base DataFrame is cached and materialized so each timing measures only the fee computation, not data generation.

Step 2: The plain UDF run serializes each of the 2,000,000 amounts from the JVM to a Python worker, multiplies by the rate, and serializes the result back. The boundary crossings dominate, so it is the slowest.

Step 3: The built-in run multiplies the column by a literal entirely inside the JVM. Catalyst fuses it into generated bytecode with no boundary crossing, so it is the fastest.

Step 4: The Pandas UDF run ships the amounts to Python in Arrow batches, so the function receives a whole pandas Series and multiplies vectorized. The boundary cost is amortized across each batch, so it is far faster than the plain UDF though still slower than the pure built-in.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Plain Python UDFs are slow in PySpark for two independent reasons, and I always name both. The first is the data-movement cost: Spark's engine runs on the JVM and columns live in efficient Tungsten binary format, but a Python UDF cannot run on the JVM, so Spark spins up Python worker processes and, for every single row, serializes the value, ships it across a process boundary over sockets, deserializes it in Python, runs the function, and serializes the result back. That per-row serialization and context switching is the dominant cost on large data. The second reason is optimizer opacity: the UDF is a sealed box to Catalyst, so it cannot push filters down to the file reader, prune columns, or fuse the operation into generated bytecode, which means even the surrounding plan gets worse.

That is why the performance hierarchy goes built-in functions first, then vectorized Pandas UDFs, then plain Python UDFs last. Built-in functions run entirely on the JVM with full optimization and whole-stage code generation and never cross the boundary, so they are fastest by a wide margin. Pandas UDFs use Apache Arrow to transfer data in batches and hand my function a whole pandas Series, so the boundary cost is amortized across many rows and they typically run ten to a hundred times faster than a plain UDF. A plain Python UDF is my last resort, only for genuinely row-wise Python logic that has no built-in or vectorized equivalent.

At the National Bank of India this came up when a developer computed a transaction fee with a plain Python UDF and the job crawled on millions of rows. I rewrote the simple multiply as a built-in column expression, amount times a literal rate, which stayed on the JVM and ran almost instantly. For a different piece of logic that truly needed a Python library, I used a Pandas UDF with Arrow enabled and got most of the speed back while keeping the custom code. The rule I repeat in interviews is: express it with built-ins if you possibly can, reach for a Pandas UDF when you need real Python, and only write a plain UDF when neither of those will do.

answers.shortTitle: Pandas UDF (vectorized UDF)

s1_definition.profdef: A Pandas UDF, also called a vectorized UDF, is a PySpark user-defined function that operates on batches of data instead of one row at a time. Spark uses Apache Arrow to transfer a column of values as a pandas Series to the Python worker, your function processes the whole Series with vectorized pandas or NumPy operations, and the result Series is shipped back via Arrow. This amortizes the JVM-to-Python boundary cost across many rows, giving a 10 to 100 times speedup over a plain row-at-a-time Python UDF. Arrow is enabled by setting `spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled` to true.
s1_definition.analogy: A plain UDF mails the National Bank's transactions to a Python analyst one letter at a time, paying postage on each. A Pandas UDF ships a whole box of transactions at once; the analyst processes the entire box with a single sweep and ships the box back. Same work, almost no postage per item, so it finishes far faster.
s1_definition.oneliner: A Pandas UDF processes a whole column at once via Arrow batches as a pandas Series, turning per-row overhead into per-batch overhead.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Pandas UDF, also called a vectorized UDF, is a PySpark user-defined function that operates on batches of data instead of one row at a time. Spark uses Apache Arrow to transfer a column of values as a pandas Series to the Python worker, your function processes the whole Series with vectorized pandas or NumPy operations, and the result Series is shipped back via Arrow. This amortizes the JVM-to-Python boundary cost across many rows, giving a 10 to 100 times speedup over a plain row-at-a-time Python UDF. Arrow is enabled by setting `spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled` to true.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A plain UDF mails the National Bank's transactions to a Python analyst one letter at a time, paying postage on each. A Pandas UDF ships a whole box of transactions at once; the analyst processes the entire box with a single sweep and ships the box back. Same work, almost no postage per item, so it finishes far faster.

**One line to remember:** A Pandas UDF processes a whole column at once via Arrow batches as a pandas Series, turning per-row overhead into per-batch overhead.

sections.s2_technical:
The slowness of a plain UDF comes from serializing and crossing the JVM-to-Python boundary for every row. A Pandas UDF fixes the mechanism: Apache Arrow is a columnar in-memory format that both the JVM and Python understand without converting object by object. Spark groups rows into batches, encodes each batch in Arrow, hands it to Python as a pandas Series, and your function runs vectorized operations over the entire Series at C speed.

You declare one with the `pandas_udf` decorator and a return type: `@pandas_udf(DoubleType())` followed by `def fee(amount: pd.Series) -> pd.Series: return amount * 0.001`. There are several flavors. A Series-to-Series UDF maps one or more input columns to one output column. A Series-to-scalar UDF is used as an aggregate, for example `@pandas_udf(DoubleType())` with `def mean_amt(a: pd.Series) -> float: return a.mean()` used in `groupBy(...).agg(mean_amt("amount"))`. An iterator-of-Series UDF lets you initialize an expensive resource once per partition, for example loading a model, then process many batches.

To enable the Arrow transfer you set `spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled` to true, either in `spark-defaults.conf` or at runtime with `spark.conf.set("spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled", "true")`. You can also tune the batch size with `spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch`. If Arrow is disabled or an unsupported type appears, Spark falls back to slower non-Arrow conversion, so you confirm it is on.

A senior nuance: Pandas UDFs still cannot be optimized through by Catalyst the way built-ins can, so a built-in expression is still faster when one exists. Use Pandas UDFs when you need genuine Python or a library like NumPy, scikit-learn, or custom math that has no SQL equivalent, and prefer the iterator form when there is expensive per-partition setup.

Problem 2 — The risk team also needs a per-account average exposure, computed with a custom aggregate. This is exactly the Series-to-scalar Pandas UDF used inside groupBy.

Problem 3 — A later model-scoring step loads a heavy scoring object that is expensive to build. This is exactly the iterator-of-Series form, which initializes once per partition.

```python
# File: src/pandas_udf_demo.py
# Demonstrates vectorized Pandas UDFs for risk scoring at the National Bank of India.
import logging
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
from scoring.risk_udfs import risk_score_udf, avg_amount_udf, scaled_score_iter

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("PandasUdfDemo")

def spark_session() -> SparkSession:
    spark = (SparkSession.builder.appName("PandasUdfDemo")
             .config("spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled", "true")
             .getOrCreate())
    log.info("Arrow enabled: %s",
             spark.conf.get("spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled"))
    return spark

def main() -> None:
    spark = spark_session()
    txns = spark.createDataFrame(
        [("TXN-1", "SAV2001", 50000.0), ("TXN-2", "CUR3001", 25000.0),
         ("TXN-3", "SAV2001", 12000.0), ("TXN-4", "CUR3001", 90000.0)],
        ["txn_id", "account_id", "amount"])

    # Series -> Series: vectorized risk score over the whole amount column
    scored = txns.withColumn("risk_score", risk_score_udf("amount"))
    log.info("Vectorized risk scores:")
    scored.show()

    # Series -> scalar: custom aggregate per account
    avg = txns.groupBy("account_id").agg(avg_amount_udf("amount").alias("avg_amt"))
    log.info("Per-account average amount (Pandas UDF aggregate):")
    avg.show()

    # Iterator-of-Series: expensive setup once per partition
    iter_scored = txns.withColumn("scaled", scaled_score_iter("amount"))
    log.info("Iterator-UDF scaled scores:")
    iter_scored.show()
    spark.stop()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```python
# File: src/scoring/risk_udfs.py
from typing import Iterator
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from pyspark.sql.functions import pandas_udf
from pyspark.sql.types import DoubleType

# Series -> Series: operates on an entire pandas Series per Arrow batch
@pandas_udf(DoubleType())
def risk_score_udf(amount: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    # vectorized NumPy: no Spark built-in equivalent for this custom formula
    return pd.Series(np.log1p(amount.to_numpy()) * 1.5)

# Series -> scalar: used as a custom aggregate inside groupBy().agg()
@pandas_udf(DoubleType())
def avg_amount_udf(amount: pd.Series) -> float:
    return float(amount.mean())

# Iterator-of-Series: build an expensive resource ONCE, reuse across batches
@pandas_udf(DoubleType())
def scaled_score_iter(it: Iterator[pd.Series]) -> Iterator[pd.Series]:
    scaler = 0.0001          # pretend this is an expensive-to-load model/config
    for batch in it:
        yield batch * scaler
```

Input data: four transactions with amounts for Rajesh and Priya.

Step 1: The SparkSession is built with Arrow enabled, and the demo logs the setting to confirm the fast path is active.

Step 2: For the Series-to-Series risk score, Spark groups the amount column into Arrow batches and hands each to Python as a pandas Series. The function applies `np.log1p(amount) * 1.5` vectorized over the whole Series and returns it. The result becomes the `risk_score` column.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A Pandas UDF, or vectorized UDF, is a PySpark function that works on batches of data rather than one row at a time. The mechanism is Apache Arrow, a columnar in-memory format both the JVM and Python understand without converting value by value. Spark groups rows into batches, encodes each batch in Arrow, hands it to the Python worker as a pandas Series, my function runs vectorized pandas or NumPy operations over the whole Series, and the result comes back the same way. Because the expensive JVM-to-Python boundary crossing now happens once per batch instead of once per row, a Pandas UDF is typically ten to a hundred times faster than a plain row-at-a-time Python UDF.

There are a few flavors I use depending on the shape of the work. A Series-to-Series UDF maps input columns to an output column and is my default for custom row-wise math. A Series-to-scalar UDF acts as a custom aggregate inside groupBy and agg, for example a mean or a custom exposure metric per account. And an iterator-of-Series UDF lets me build an expensive resource like a loaded model once per partition and then process many batches with it, which avoids repeating costly setup. I enable the fast path by setting spark dot sql dot execution dot arrow dot pyspark dot enabled to true, and I can tune the batch size with maxRecordsPerBatch.

At the National Bank of India I reached for Pandas UDFs whenever the logic needed real Python with no Spark built-in equivalent. A custom risk-scoring formula that used a NumPy function ran far too slowly as a plain UDF, so I rewrote it as a Series-to-Series Pandas UDF and it processed millions of transactions in a fraction of the time. I used the Series-to-scalar form for a custom per-account average and the iterator form when a later step loaded a heavy scoring object. The important caveat I always add is that a Pandas UDF still cannot be optimized through by Catalyst, so if a pure built-in expression exists I use that first, and I only reach for a Pandas UDF when I genuinely need Python.

answers.question: What are Spark's complex/nested data types — `StructType` (nested record/object), `ArrayType` (list of elements), `MapType` (key-value dictionary) — and how do you access them (dot notation for structs, `getItem`/bracket for arrays/maps, `explode()` to flatten arrays)?
answers.shortTitle: Spark complex/nested data types — StructType, ArrayType, MapType

s1_definition.profdef: Spark supports nested/complex column types in addition to scalars. `StructType` represents a nested record or object with named fields, like a JSON object. `ArrayType` represents an ordered list of elements of a single element type. `MapType` represents a dictionary of key-value pairs. You access a struct field with dot notation or `getField`, an array element with `getItem` or bracket indexing, and a map value by key; you flatten an array into multiple rows with `explode`.
s1_definition.analogy: A customer record at the National Bank is not flat. Each customer has an address object with street and city (a StructType), a list of recent transactions (an ArrayType), and a set of named limits like daily and monthly caps (a MapType). Spark lets you store all of this in one row and reach into it: address.city for the struct, transactions[0] for the first in the list, limits['daily'] for a named value, and explode to turn the transaction list into one row per transaction.
s1_definition.oneliner: StructType is a nested object, ArrayType is a list, MapType is a dictionary; use dot notation for structs, getItem/brackets for arrays and maps, and explode to flatten arrays into rows.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Spark supports nested/complex column types in addition to scalars. `StructType` represents a nested record or object with named fields, like a JSON object. `ArrayType` represents an ordered list of elements of a single element type. `MapType` represents a dictionary of key-value pairs. You access a struct field with dot notation or `getField`, an array element with `getItem` or bracket indexing, and a map value by key; you flatten an array into multiple rows with `explode`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A customer record at the National Bank is not flat. Each customer has an address object with street and city (a StructType), a list of recent transactions (an ArrayType), and a set of named limits like daily and monthly caps (a MapType). Spark lets you store all of this in one row and reach into it: address.city for the struct, transactions[0] for the first in the list, limits['daily'] for a named value, and explode to turn the transaction list into one row per transaction.

**One line to remember:** StructType is a nested object, ArrayType is a list, MapType is a dictionary; use dot notation for structs, getItem/brackets for arrays and maps, and explode to flatten arrays into rows.

sections.s2_technical:
A `StructType` is a schema of named, typed fields and is how Spark models nested JSON objects and sub-records. If a column `address` is a struct with fields `street` and `city`, you read a field with dot notation `F.col("address.city")` or `df.select("address.city")`, and you build one with `F.struct(F.col("street"), F.col("city")).alias("address")`.

An `ArrayType` holds an ordered list of elements of one type, such as an array of strings or an array of structs. You read an element by position with `F.col("tags").getItem(0)` or `F.col("tags")[0]`, get its length with `F.size("tags")`, test membership with `F.array_contains("tags", "VIP")`, and flatten it into rows with `F.explode("tags")`, which produces one output row per element.

A `MapType` holds key-value pairs where keys share one type and values share another, like a dictionary. You read a value by key with `F.col("limits")["daily"]` or `F.col("limits").getItem("daily")`, extract all keys with `F.map_keys("limits")`, all values with `F.map_values("limits")`, and flatten into key and value columns with `F.explode("limits")`.

These types compose freely: an array of structs, a map whose values are arrays, a struct containing an array. Spark reads them natively from JSON, Parquet, Avro, and Delta, preserving nesting. For writing, columnar formats like Parquet store nested data efficiently. A senior nuance is that `explode` multiplies rows, so you select and filter before exploding to avoid blowing up intermediate data, and for simple element-wise work you often prefer higher-order functions over exploding.

```python
def main() -> None:

    schema = StructType([
        StructField("account_id", StringType()),
        StructField("address", StructType([                 # StructType
            StructField("street", StringType()),
            StructField("city", StringType())])),
        StructField("recent_txns", ArrayType(DoubleType())),# ArrayType
        StructField("limits", MapType(StringType(), DoubleType())),  # MapType
```

```python
# File: src/access/nested_access.py
from pyspark.sql import DataFrame, functions as F

class NestedAccess:
    """Reads into StructType/ArrayType/MapType columns."""
    def __init__(self, df: DataFrame):
        self.df = df

    def scalars(self) -> DataFrame:
        return self.df.select(
            "account_id",
            F.col("address.city").alias("city"),          # struct: dot notation
            F.col("recent_txns").getItem(0).alias("first_txn"),  # array: getItem
            F.col("limits")["daily"].alias("daily_limit"),       # map: bracket by key
            F.size("recent_txns").alias("txn_count"))

    def exploded_txns(self) -> DataFrame:
        # SELECT + account_id BEFORE explode to limit row multiplication
        return (self.df.select("account_id", "recent_txns")
                .withColumn("txn_amount", F.explode("recent_txns"))
                .drop("recent_txns"))
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Spark supports complex, nested column types alongside the usual scalars, and I use three of them constantly. StructType is a nested record with named, typed fields, which is how Spark models a JSON object or a sub-record like an address with street and city. ArrayType is an ordered list of elements of a single type, like a list of transaction amounts. MapType is a dictionary of key-value pairs, like a set of named spending limits. These compose freely, so I can have an array of structs or a map of arrays, and Spark reads and writes the nesting natively in JSON, Parquet, Avro, and Delta.

Accessing them follows a simple set of rules. For a struct I use dot notation, so address.city or col of address dot city reads the field. For an array I use getItem or bracket indexing by position, size for the length, and array_contains to test membership. For a map I read a value by key with bracket notation or getItem, and I can pull all keys or all values with map_keys and map_values. When I need to turn an array into individual rows, I use explode, which produces one output row per element, and explode_outer if I want to keep rows whose array is null or empty.

At the National Bank of India this mattered because our customer API returned deeply nested JSON: an address object, a list of recent transactions, and a map of limits. Instead of flattening everything on ingest and losing structure, I kept the nesting and reached into it on demand — dot notation for the city, getItem for the first transaction, and a map key for the daily limit — and I exploded the transaction array only when the risk team needed one row per transaction. The practical rule I always state is to select and filter before exploding, because explode multiplies rows and every column you carry through gets multiplied with them.

answers.question: What is `explode()` vs `explode_outer()` — `explode` drops rows where the array is null/empty, `explode_outer` keeps them with nulls — and why should you filter and select BEFORE exploding (every row and column before the explode gets multiplied)?
answers.shortTitle: explode() vs explode_outer()

s1_definition.profdef: `explode` and `explode_outer` both flatten an array (or map) column into multiple rows, producing one output row per element. The difference is null handling: `explode` drops a row entirely if its array is null or empty, so those parent rows disappear, whereas `explode_outer` keeps such rows, emitting a single row with a null in the exploded column. You should select only needed columns and filter before exploding because every surviving parent row and every carried column is duplicated once per array element, so exploding early multiplies data you did not need.
s1_definition.analogy: Each National Bank customer has a list of recent transactions. Exploding turns one customer row into one row per transaction. With `explode`, a customer who made no transactions (empty list) vanishes from the result, which can silently drop customers from a report. With `explode_outer`, that customer still appears once with a null transaction, so you keep everyone. And because exploding copies the customer's other columns onto every transaction row, you trim to only the columns you need first, or you waste memory copying everything.
s1_definition.oneliner: explode drops rows with null or empty arrays, explode_outer keeps them with nulls, and you filter and select before exploding because every parent row and column gets multiplied.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `explode` and `explode_outer` both flatten an array (or map) column into multiple rows, producing one output row per element. The difference is null handling: `explode` drops a row entirely if its array is null or empty, so those parent rows disappear, whereas `explode_outer` keeps such rows, emitting a single row with a null in the exploded column. You should select only needed columns and filter before exploding because every surviving parent row and every carried column is duplicated once per array element, so exploding early multiplies data you did not need.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Each National Bank customer has a list of recent transactions. Exploding turns one customer row into one row per transaction. With `explode`, a customer who made no transactions (empty list) vanishes from the result, which can silently drop customers from a report. With `explode_outer`, that customer still appears once with a null transaction, so you keep everyone. And because exploding copies the customer's other columns onto every transaction row, you trim to only the columns you need first, or you waste memory copying everything.

**One line to remember:** explode drops rows with null or empty arrays, explode_outer keeps them with nulls, and you filter and select before exploding because every parent row and column gets multiplied.

sections.s2_technical:
`F.explode(col)` takes an array column and produces one row per element, copying the other columns of the parent row onto each new row. If the array is null or empty, the parent row contributes zero rows to the output, so it is dropped. This behaves like an inner join between the row and its array elements.

`F.explode_outer(col)` is the left-outer equivalent: for a null or empty array it still emits one row for that parent with null in the exploded column, so no parent row is lost. The same pair exists for maps, where exploding yields key and value columns. There is also `posexplode` and `posexplode_outer`, which additionally emit the element's position index.

The choice matters for correctness. If a report must count every customer, using `explode` silently removes customers with no transactions, understating totals, so `explode_outer` is the safe default when parent rows must be preserved. If you only care about actual elements, `explode` is correct and smaller.

The performance guidance is about row and column multiplication. Explode is a one-to-many operation: a parent row with ten elements becomes ten rows, and every column you carried through is copied ten times. If you explode first and then select or filter, Spark materializes a wide, multiplied intermediate before discarding columns and rows. If instead you select only the columns you need and filter out rows you will discard before exploding, the multiplication applies to a much smaller, narrower dataset. For example `df.select("account_id", "recent_txns").filter(F.size("recent_txns") > 0).withColumn("amt", F.explode("recent_txns"))` keeps the intermediate tight.

A senior nuance: when the parent has several arrays, exploding each separately can create a cross-product explosion, so you either `arrays_zip` them first or explode one and handle the others with higher-order functions to avoid an accidental blow-up.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank's monthly statement report flattens each customer's transaction array into individual lines. A new customer with no transactions this month was silently dropped from the report because the team used `explode`. The auditors flagged the missing customer. This is exactly the explode-versus-explode_outer correctness issue.

Problem 2 — The customer records carry many wide columns (address, KYC fields). Exploding before trimming copied all of them onto every transaction line, wasting memory. This is exactly why we select before exploding.

Problem 3 — The report must include customers with zero transactions showing a null line. This is exactly what explode_outer provides.

```python
# File: src/flatten/statement_flattener.py
from pyspark.sql import DataFrame, functions as F

class StatementFlattener:
    """Flattens transaction arrays into statement lines."""
    def __init__(self, df: DataFrame):
        self.df = df

    def inner_explode(self) -> DataFrame:
        # SELECT only needed columns BEFORE exploding (drop wide 'kyc')
        trimmed = self.df.select("account_id", "recent_txns")
        return trimmed.withColumn("txn_amount", F.explode("recent_txns")) \
                      .drop("recent_txns")

    def outer_explode(self) -> DataFrame:
        trimmed = self.df.select("account_id", "recent_txns")
        return trimmed.withColumn("txn_amount", F.explode_outer("recent_txns")) \
                      .drop("recent_txns")
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Both explode and explode_outer flatten an array or map column into multiple rows, emitting one output row per element and copying the parent row's other columns onto each new row. The difference is purely how they treat a null or empty array. Explode behaves like an inner join between the row and its elements, so a parent whose array is null or empty contributes zero rows and disappears from the result. Explode_outer behaves like a left-outer join, so that same parent still produces one row with a null in the exploded column and is never lost. There are posexplode variants too, which also give you the element's position index.

The choice is a correctness decision, not just a style preference. If a report must account for every customer, using explode silently drops customers who happened to have no transactions, which understates totals and gets flagged in an audit. So when parent rows must be preserved, explode_outer is the safe default, and I reserve plain explode for when I only care about actual elements and dropping empties is intended.

The performance guidance I always apply is to select and filter before exploding, because explode is a one-to-many operation. A parent row with ten elements becomes ten rows, and every column I carry through is copied ten times. If I explode first and trim later, Spark builds a wide, multiplied intermediate and then throws most of it away. At the National Bank of India our statement job once used explode and silently dropped a new customer with zero transactions, which the auditors caught, so we switched to explode_outer and also moved the column selection ahead of the explode so the heavy KYC fields were never copied onto every transaction line. The sentence I memorize is: explode drops null and empty arrays, explode_outer keeps them as nulls, and always trim and filter before you explode.

answers.question: What are higher-order array functions — `transform`, `filter`, `aggregate`, `exists`, `forall` (Spark 2.4+) — that let you operate on array elements WITHOUT exploding, and when are they preferred (avoid row multiplication for simple transforms/checks)?
answers.shortTitle: Higher-order array functions — transform, filter, aggregate, exists, forall

s1_definition.profdef: Higher-order array functions, introduced in Spark 2.4, let you operate on the elements of an array column in place, passing a lambda expression, without exploding the array into rows. `transform` maps each element to a new value, `filter` keeps elements matching a predicate, `aggregate` folds elements into a single value with an accumulator, `exists` returns true if any element matches, and `forall` returns true if all elements match. They are preferred over explode for element-wise transforms and checks because they avoid the row multiplication and later regrouping that exploding forces.
s1_definition.analogy: Each National Bank customer row holds a list of transaction amounts. If you want to add a fee to every amount, find the big ones, total them, or check whether any is suspicious, you do not need to scatter the list into separate rows and gather them back. Higher-order functions do the work right inside the list while it stays in one row: transform adds the fee to each, filter keeps the big ones, aggregate totals them, exists checks for any suspicious amount, and forall checks they are all within limit.
s1_definition.oneliner: Higher-order array functions (transform, filter, aggregate, exists, forall) process array elements in place with a lambda, avoiding the explode-then-regroup cost.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Higher-order array functions, introduced in Spark 2.4, let you operate on the elements of an array column in place, passing a lambda expression, without exploding the array into rows. `transform` maps each element to a new value, `filter` keeps elements matching a predicate, `aggregate` folds elements into a single value with an accumulator, `exists` returns true if any element matches, and `forall` returns true if all elements match. They are preferred over explode for element-wise transforms and checks because they avoid the row multiplication and later regrouping that exploding forces.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Each National Bank customer row holds a list of transaction amounts. If you want to add a fee to every amount, find the big ones, total them, or check whether any is suspicious, you do not need to scatter the list into separate rows and gather them back. Higher-order functions do the work right inside the list while it stays in one row: transform adds the fee to each, filter keeps the big ones, aggregate totals them, exists checks for any suspicious amount, and forall checks they are all within limit.

**One line to remember:** Higher-order array functions (transform, filter, aggregate, exists, forall) process array elements in place with a lambda, avoiding the explode-then-regroup cost.

sections.s2_technical:
Before Spark 2.4 the common way to transform array elements was to explode the array, apply an operation, then group back, which multiplied rows and added a shuffle. Higher-order functions keep the array intact and apply a lambda to its elements inside the single row, so there is no multiplication and no regroup.

`transform(array, x -> expr)` returns a new array where each element is the result of the lambda, for example `F.transform("amounts", lambda x: x * 1.001)` adds a fee to each amount. `filter(array, x -> predicate)` returns a new array containing only elements where the predicate is true, for example `F.filter("amounts", lambda x: x > 50000)` keeps large amounts. `aggregate(array, start, (acc, x) -> expr [, acc -> finish])` folds the array into one value, for example `F.aggregate("amounts", F.lit(0.0), lambda acc, x: acc + x)` sums it. `exists(array, x -> predicate)` returns a boolean true if any element satisfies the predicate, for example `F.exists("amounts", lambda x: x > 1000000)` flags a very large transaction. `forall(array, x -> predicate)` returns true only if every element satisfies it, for example `F.forall("amounts", lambda x: x > 0)` checks all amounts are positive.

In the PySpark API from Spark 3.1 onward these accept Python lambdas directly; in SQL you write the arrow syntax, for example `transform(amounts, x -> x * 1.001)`. They compose: you can filter then transform then aggregate in one expression chain, all staying columnar on the JVM with no Python boundary and no row explosion.

A senior nuance: prefer higher-order functions for element-wise work and simple reductions because they keep the plan narrow and let Catalyst optimize. Reach for explode only when you genuinely need each element as its own row, for example to join elements against another table or to produce per-element output rows.

Problem 3 — All of this must happen without scattering the list into rows, keeping one row per customer. This is the core benefit of higher-order functions.

```python
# File: src/arrays/array_ops.py
from pyspark.sql import DataFrame, functions as F

class ArrayOps:
    """Applies higher-order array functions in place (no explode)."""
    def __init__(self, df: DataFrame):
        self.df = df

    def enrich(self) -> DataFrame:
        return self.df.select(
            "account_id",
            # transform: add a 0.1% fee to EACH element
            F.transform("amounts", lambda x: x * 1.001).alias("with_fee"),
            # filter: keep only large transactions
            F.filter("amounts", lambda x: x > 50000).alias("large_txns"),
            # aggregate: fold the array into a single total
            F.aggregate("amounts", F.lit(0.0), lambda acc, x: acc + x).alias("total"),
            # exists: true if ANY transaction is huge
            F.exists("amounts", lambda x: x > 1000000).alias("has_huge"),
            # forall: true only if ALL amounts are positive
            F.forall("amounts", lambda x: x > 0).alias("all_positive"))
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: SAV2001 with amounts [50000, 12000, 1200000] and CUR3001 with [25000, 90000].

Step 1: `transform` applies the lambda `x * 1.001` to each element in place, so SAV2001's array becomes each amount plus a 0.1% fee, still as one array in one row.

Step 2: `filter` keeps only elements greater than 50000. SAV2001 keeps [1200000] (12000 and 50000 are not strictly greater), CUR3001 keeps [90000].

Step 3: `aggregate` folds each array starting from 0.0, summing elements. SAV2001 totals 1,262,000; CUR3001 totals 115,000.

Step 4: `exists` checks whether any element exceeds 1,000,000. SAV2001 is true because of 1,200,000; CUR3001 is false.

Step 5: `forall` checks all elements are positive. Both are true. All five results sit on the same single row per customer, with no explode and no regroup shuffle.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Higher-order array functions, which arrived in Spark 2.4, let me operate on the elements of an array column in place by passing a lambda, without ever exploding the array into rows. The five I use most are transform, which maps each element to a new value; filter, which keeps only elements matching a predicate; aggregate, which folds the elements into a single value with an accumulator and an optional finisher; exists, which returns true if any element matches; and forall, which returns true only if every element matches. In the PySpark API from Spark 3.1 I pass Python lambdas directly, and in SQL I use the arrow syntax like transform of amounts comma x arrow x times 1.001.

The reason I prefer them over explode for element-wise work is cost. Before these functions existed, the pattern was to explode the array, do the operation, and group back, which multiplied rows and added a shuffle. Higher-order functions keep the array in one row, apply the lambda columnar on the JVM, and produce either a new array or a scalar, so there is no multiplication and no regroup. They also compose freely, so I can filter then transform then aggregate in a single expression, and Catalyst can optimize the whole thing because nothing crosses into Python.

At the National Bank of India this cleaned up our feature engineering. For each customer's transaction list I added a processing fee to every amount with transform, pulled out the large transactions with filter, totalled the list with aggregate, flagged whether any single amount was suspiciously large with exists, and confirmed all amounts were positive with forall, all while keeping exactly one row per customer. The guidance I give in interviews is to use higher-order functions for element-wise maps, checks, and simple reductions, and to reach for explode only when I genuinely need each element as its own row, such as joining elements against another table.

answers.question: What is SparkContext vs SparkSession — SparkContext (Spark 1.x entry point, manages RDDs, cluster connection; only one per JVM) vs SparkSession (Spark 2.0+ unified entry point, wraps SparkContext + SQLContext + HiveContext; access SparkContext via `spark.sparkContext`) — and why is SparkSession the modern standard?
answers.shortTitle: SparkContext vs SparkSession

s1_definition.profdef: SparkContext is the original Spark 1.x entry point that represents the connection to the cluster and the low-level API for creating and manipulating RDDs; there can be only one active SparkContext per JVM. SparkSession, introduced in Spark 2.0, is the unified entry point that wraps SparkContext together with the old SQLContext and HiveContext, giving a single object for DataFrames, Datasets, Spark SQL, and catalog access. You still get the underlying SparkContext through `spark.sparkContext`. SparkSession is the modern standard because it unifies all these entry points and is the handle for the optimized DataFrame and SQL APIs.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of SparkContext as the old single phone line into the National Bank's data-processing cluster — essential, but low level, and you can only have one line per building. SparkSession is the modern reception desk that still has that phone line behind it but also handles SQL requests, table lookups, and DataFrame work through one friendly front door. Developers call the reception desk now, not the raw phone line.
s1_definition.oneliner: SparkContext is the low-level RDD and cluster connection (one per JVM); SparkSession is the modern unified front door that wraps it and adds DataFrames, SQL, and catalog.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** SparkContext is the original Spark 1.x entry point that represents the connection to the cluster and the low-level API for creating and manipulating RDDs; there can be only one active SparkContext per JVM. SparkSession, introduced in Spark 2.0, is the unified entry point that wraps SparkContext together with the old SQLContext and HiveContext, giving a single object for DataFrames, Datasets, Spark SQL, and catalog access. You still get the underlying SparkContext through `spark.sparkContext`. SparkSession is the modern standard because it unifies all these entry points and is the handle for the optimized DataFrame and SQL APIs.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of SparkContext as the old single phone line into the National Bank's data-processing cluster — essential, but low level, and you can only have one line per building. SparkSession is the modern reception desk that still has that phone line behind it but also handles SQL requests, table lookups, and DataFrame work through one friendly front door. Developers call the reception desk now, not the raw phone line.

**One line to remember:** SparkContext is the low-level RDD and cluster connection (one per JVM); SparkSession is the modern unified front door that wraps it and adds DataFrames, SQL, and catalog.

sections.s2_technical:
In Spark 1.x the entry point was SparkContext, created from a SparkConf, and it was how you connected to the cluster manager, requested executors, and created RDDs with methods like `parallelize` and `textFile`. To use SQL or structured data you also needed a separate SQLContext, and to use Hive tables a HiveContext, so applications juggled several context objects. There can be only one active SparkContext per JVM because it owns the cluster connection and scheduler.

Spark 2.0 introduced SparkSession as a single unified entry point. You build it with `SparkSession.builder.appName("...").getOrCreate()`, and it internally holds a SparkContext plus the functionality previously split across SQLContext and HiveContext. Through it you create DataFrames and Datasets, run `spark.sql("...")`, read sources with `spark.read`, and access the metadata catalog with `spark.catalog`. When you still need the low-level API — for example `parallelize`, accumulators, broadcast variables, or setting a log level — you reach the wrapped context with `spark.sparkContext`.

SparkSession is the modern standard for several reasons. It unifies the fragmented contexts into one object, so there is less boilerplate and no confusion about which context to use. It is the handle for the DataFrame and Dataset APIs, which run through the Catalyst optimizer and Tungsten execution engine and are far faster and more optimizable than hand-written RDD code. It supports multiple isolated sessions sharing one SparkContext via `newSession`, which is useful for multi-tenant applications. And `getOrCreate` safely reuses an existing session, avoiding accidental duplicate contexts.

A senior nuance: RDDs and SparkContext are not gone — SparkSession is built on them, and you drop to the RDD level for fine-grained control or legacy code — but new code should be written against SparkSession and DataFrames so it benefits from the optimizer.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A legacy National Bank job was written in Spark 1.x style with a SparkContext creating RDDs and a separate SQLContext for queries, which was clumsy and slow. This is exactly the fragmentation SparkSession removes.

Problem 2 — The modernized job needs one entry point for DataFrames, SQL, and reading files, yet still occasionally needs the low-level context for a broadcast variable. This is exactly SparkSession plus `spark.sparkContext`.

Problem 3 — The team wants the optimizer to accelerate queries. This is exactly why DataFrames through SparkSession beat raw RDDs.

What the code will do: a PySpark demo (`SessionDemo`) that creates a SparkSession, uses it for a DataFrame of accounts for Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001), runs a Spark SQL query, and reaches the underlying SparkContext for a broadcast and the app id.

```python
# File: src/session_demo.py
# Shows SparkSession as the unified entry point for the National Bank of India.
import logging
from decimal import Decimal
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from runtime.spark_factory import build_session

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("SessionDemo")

def main() -> None:
    spark = build_session()                      # unified entry point
    sc = spark.sparkContext                       # underlying low-level context
    log.info("App id via SparkContext: %s", sc.applicationId)

    # DataFrame API through SparkSession (optimized by Catalyst)
    accounts = spark.createDataFrame(
        [("SAV2001", "Rajesh Kumar", Decimal("1000000.00")),
         ("CUR3001", "Priya Sharma", Decimal("250000.00"))],
        ["account_id", "holder_name", "balance"])
    accounts.createOrReplaceTempView("accounts")

    # Spark SQL through the SAME session (was a separate SQLContext in 1.x)
    rich = spark.sql("SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts WHERE balance > 300000")
    log.info("Spark SQL result (balance > 300000):")
    rich.show()

    # Low-level API via spark.sparkContext: broadcast a fee rate
    fee_rate = sc.broadcast(0.001)
    log.info("Broadcast fee rate value: %s", fee_rate.value)

    # RDD access still available underneath the DataFrame
    log.info("Partitions in accounts RDD: %d", accounts.rdd.getNumPartitions())
    spark.stop()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```python
# File: src/runtime/spark_factory.py
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

def build_session() -> SparkSession:
    # getOrCreate reuses an existing session (avoids duplicate SparkContext)
    return (SparkSession.builder
            .appName("SessionDemo")
            .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "8")
            .getOrCreate())
```

SparkContext is the original Spark 1.x entry point. It represents the connection to the cluster and the low-level API for creating and manipulating RDDs, and there can be only one active SparkContext per JVM because it owns the cluster connection and the scheduler. In that era, to do SQL you needed a separate SQLContext, and to touch Hive tables you needed a HiveContext, so applications juggled several context objects. SparkSession, introduced in Spark 2.0, is the unified entry point that wraps a SparkContext together with the old SQLContext and HiveContext behind one object, and when I still need the low-level API I reach the underlying context through spark dot sparkContext.

SparkSession is the modern standard for concrete reasons. It unifies the fragmented contexts into one handle, so there is no boilerplate and no confusion about which context to use. It is the entry point for the DataFrame and Dataset APIs, which run through the Catalyst optimizer and the Tungsten engine and are far faster and more optimizable than hand-written RDD code. It supports multiple isolated sessions sharing one SparkContext through newSession for multi-tenant apps, and getOrCreate safely reuses an existing session so I never accidentally create a duplicate context.

At the National Bank of India I modernized a legacy Spark 1.x job that mixed a SparkContext for RDDs with a separate SQLContext for queries. I replaced all of that with a single SparkSession built through getOrCreate, moved the logic to DataFrames and spark dot sql so the optimizer could accelerate it, and only dropped to spark dot sparkContext when I genuinely needed the low-level API, like broadcasting a fee rate.
